release_focus: Sharp shared-query guarantees and source-derived minimum fixed reading budgets.
title: Adaptive Reading Budgets for Joint Forecast Audits with Cumulative Data
abstract:
Background. Model audits share verification readings across several predictors. We ask how many readings suffice for precise comparisons and when choosing later readings after earlier answers reduces this requirement.

Methods. We study sharp intervals for affine model-loss contrasts on compact convex sets using a finite query dictionary. We prove fixed-budget bounds, compute minimum fixed reading budgets, and replay certified policies on cumulative-meter data.

Results. For one comparison, if a deterministic policy guarantees precision with two exact scalar readings, some randomized fixed batch succeeds with worst-case probability at least 1/2. This lower bound disappears with two comparisons. For every m>=3, we construct instances where adaptation always succeeds but the best randomized batch succeeds with worst-case probability exactly 1/m. All coordinates are queryable, the budget remains two, and each comparison is separately certifiable by a fixed batch. The separation also holds for all pairwise comparisons among three models. On 225 of 1,098 meter blocks across six systems, two adaptive readings guarantee halving every comparison's width, while the minimum fixed budget is three. Of these, 222 have optimal randomized two-reading batch success exactly 1/2. The one-third reading reduction on qualifying blocks becomes 6.40% and 7.67% across the complete original and external panels. Capacity information reduces the advantage, and measured public-API retrieval favors bulk.

Conclusions. Sharing a reading budget can make feedback necessary for assurance even when separate comparisons need none. The construction proves a fixed-budget boundary; the retrospective meter study quantifies its narrower benefit in required readings, separately from retrieval cost.
